summary: This best current practice document describes the reservation of Autonomous System Numbers for private use and gives operational guidance. It enlarges the private use space by documenting a second, larger reserved range. It updates RFC 1930 by replacing Section 10.

plainLanguage.summary: Some network ID numbers are set aside for private use, like internal room numbers. This adds a much bigger set.

subtitle: Reserves a second, much larger block of private AS numbers for networks that do not need globally unique ones.

tldr.problem: The original block of 1023 Private Use AS numbers was too small for new BGP uses such as data center networks, and it could not be renumbered because private numbers are not registered.
tldr.mechanism: IANA keeps the old range 64512 - 65534 and reserves a second range, 4200000000 - 4294967294, from the four-octet AS number space.
tldr.outcome: Operators get far more private AS numbers, but must strip them from AS paths before routes reach the global Internet.

today: RFC 6996 is a Best Current Practice and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 1930.

sections.title: Why a Bigger Private Range
sections.content:
The original IANA reservation of Private Use Autonomous System Numbers (ASNs) was a block of 1023 numbers, also documented in RFC 1930. Since then, BGP has been deployed in new domains such as data center networks, which need a larger private space.

The four-octet AS space from RFC 6793 made the total ASN space much bigger. The existing private range is widely deployed and cannot be renumbered, because these ASNs are by definition not registered. So the RFC documents the existing reservation and adds a second, larger range.
sections.plainLanguage: The neighborhood ran out of house numbers and could not rename its streets, so a new, huge neighborhood was added next to it.

sections.title: The Two Private Use Ranges
sections.content: IANA reserved a contiguous block of 1023 numbers from the 16-bit registry, 64512 - 65534 inclusive. It also reserved a second contiguous block from the 32-bit registry, 4200000000 - 4294967294 inclusive. The first range is part of the original 16-bit space from RFC 1930, and the second is part of the four-octet space.
sections.plainLanguage: There are now two private ranges: the small old one and a large new one.

sections.title: Operational Rules
sections.content:
If prefixes originate from Private Use ASNs, those ASNs MUST be removed from AS path attributes (including AS4_PATH) before being advertised to the global Internet. Normal AS path filtering MAY also be used.

Operators SHOULD make sure all EBGP speakers support RFC 6793 and that features recognizing Private Use ASNs know both ranges before using the new range. Some implementations do not remove private ASNs when the path mixes private and non-private ones. If they do not know the new range, they will likely stop removing private ASNs from either path attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Private numbers must be taken off the label before a letter leaves your neighborhood, and your mail sorters must know about the new neighborhood first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Private Use ASNs raise no unique security concerns. Loss of connectivity might result from using them outside a single organization, since they are not globally unique, but that loss is limited to the organization doing so. Finding the originator of a route with a private ASN means tracking it back to the neighboring globally unique AS or inspecting other attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: If you use a neighborhood-only number outside the neighborhood, only you get confused.
